Make note that this asks about a binary tree, NOT a binary search tree.
In a binary search tree, the runtime complexity would be $O(\log n)$ because it goes through a single branch of the tree.
However, in a binary tree, the elements can be inserted without being sorted. Therefore it is no different than an unsorted array, therefore the runtime would be $O(n)$.

Building the heap itself from an array takes O(nlogn) time for the top down approach (it wouldve taken O(n) time if bottom up approach was used)

Doing the sorting itself once a heap is built takes O(nlogn) time

Both the heapify and the sort are part of the general HeapSort function thus we need to add them together. Video creator accidentally flipped the f and b marker, don't let that confuse you. Enqueue calls always place new items on the end with b and dequeue calls always remove items from the side with f. For the purposes of this class, the f marker is usually on the index with the item that is to be removed next and the b marker is one to the right of the most recently added item (such that the next item to be added will be added where b is).

In the best case for quick sort, we always pick the median value of an array to be our pivot index but with truly random arrays, what is the most effective way of picking the median value (without going through to find the median which creates extra overhead time)? There is none, thus there is no best policy

Any runtime expression where $\frac{1}{32} n^2$ is the term that grows the fastest with respect to n. Examples include:
$T(n)=\frac{1}{32} n^2+3n+4$
$T(n)=\frac{1}{32} n^2+25n\log{{n}}+1$
$T(n)=\frac{1}{32} n^2+\frac{8}{n}$

For Gap = 13, n = 6 so comparison never executes, 0 compares. 
Gap = 4 gives 2 compares (P < U, U < E). 
Gap = 1 gives 7 compares (U < U, U < R, R < D, D < P, R < D, D < E, P < E). Total is 9 compares.

1. P < U so swap: [U, U, R, D, P, E]
2. D < P so swap: [U, U, R, P, D, E]
3. D < E so swap: [U, U, R, P, E, D]

Therefore 3 swaps total.
